en: Preface to the *Essential Collection of the Recorded Sayings of Boshan*:
The Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is like the Vajra King’s precious sword; it is not easily obtained, not easily wielded, and not easily transmitted.
Because all these aspects are difficult, those who truly uphold this Way are indeed rare. And...
Fish eyes are mixed with pearls; mountain pheasants masquerade as phoenixes—such has been the state of half the world.

Our Caodong school flourished during the Tang dynasty and declined during the Song; by the Yuan, it appeared to flourish again yet was actually in decline. The reasons for this are difficult to articulate.

Since the early years of the Yuan dynasty, when Master Xueting Yu received the imperial decree to reside at Shaolin, scholars throughout the land have unanimously revered him as their master. This lineage was transmitted through successive generations until the first year of the Wanli era. At that time, a small...

When Mount Shu passed away, the Emperor issued an edict appointing Huànrùn to succeed him on the seat. Those from all quarters who arrived with their satchels upon their backs were like birds flocking to a forest or fish rushing to a stream;
yet Master Rùn devoted himself primarily to lecturing and commentary, which greatly disappointed the expectations of the assembly. At that time, there was Yùn...
Master Kongzhong served the Elder Xiaoshan for many years and received his secret seal.

He returned to seclusion at Lingshan in Xujiang, where no one in the world could discover his whereabouts. My late teacher Shouchang followed him in receiving the tonsure and later received his formal transmission;
only then did he begin to propagate the teachings. Once Master Lai of Boshan succeeded him, the Way flourished extensively.
In this world, the Master has long endured the hardships of ascetic practice and has fully experienced all manner of perils and obstacles;

thus, his words regarding the methods of cultivation are uniquely detailed. His light of wisdom is perfectly round and complete, and his eloquence is unimpeded. His discourse is as vast and surging as a great ocean, its depths unfathomable;

consequently, many students look upon it like the vast sea and turn back in retreat. His teaching style is strict and rigorous, distinguishing instantly between gold and brass; he holds high the ancestral seal and does not grant permission to others recklessly.
It is so. Therefore, those who borrow the melodic resonance of the "chicken" [a term for superficiality] must not recklessly cross passes and ferries, thereby confusing the ears of the multitude.
Following the passing of my late teacher, I relied upon him for three years.

Although I gained nothing from him, during those three years I never saw a single word of his that leaked into the realm of emotional consciousness; he merely exhorted me toward the matter of the Ultimate. Thus, as for my teacher—
The favor you have bestowed upon me is truly great. When I was sequestered at Mount He, the Master returned from Shigou and passed through Jianzhou on his way;
we met at Guangxiao Temple. The Master asked, "Have you swept the pagoda of Shouchang yet? I replied, "The sweeping has not been neglected."
“I simply do not permit others to know. The Master said, “If that is so, then you have been sweeping by stealth.
Yu said, “The worthy one is merely like this; what about you, Master? The Master said, “Sweeping is not neglected, but it has never been moved.
Yu said, “Then you, Master, seem as though you have not swept at all. Thereupon he laughed and took his leave. When the Master passed away, his recorded sayings were vast.
It is voluminous; spanning many volumes and filling numerous scrolls, it is difficult to circulate.

Consequently, there are those in distant regions and remote lands who have heard the Master’s name and turned toward his transformation, yet whose eyes have never once encountered his recorded sayings (*yulu*).
Since the autumn of the Renwu year, I returned to Xigu [Stone Drum] Monastery; thereupon, at the request of the monk Hunpu, I ventured to select the essential passages from the complete record.

Categorizing and synthesizing these [teachings], I have compared them with the *Complete Record* (*Quanlu*), which accounts for only one-third of the whole. Nevertheless, they are concise yet easy to practice, and succinct yet easy to realize.
If scholars throughout the world were to exhaustively investigate them, they would be able to see the entirety of the Great Whole.
May they thereby know that the Way of Boshan is so vast, profound, and subtle; it is not something that those who foolishly cling to a single peg can even vaguely imagine in its myriad aspects.
First. Alas! The "Guangling San" shall never be played again. Fortunately, its score still survives today.
How might one hear this piece once more amidst the cool breezes and white moonlight?
Written on the first day of the Lantern Festival in the first month of spring in the *guimǐn* year of the Chóngzhēn era, by the śramaṇa Yuánxián,
a transmitter of the orthodox Caodōng lineage, while residing at Yǒngquán Chan Monastery on Mount Gǔ in Fúzhòu, at his own dwelling, the Pīnshēn Studio.
